short_summary: Explore Europe's historic spa towns designated by Unesco, featuring centuries-old healing traditions, thermal springs, and architectural landmarks from Czechia to Slovenia.

sources.name: The Guardian
sources.title: Healing waters: 10 of the best spa towns in Europe for a restorative autumn break

paragraphs: Europe boasts a rich tradition of wellness tourism that reached its peak between 1700 and the 1930s. In 2021, Unesco recognized the exceptional legacy of this phenomenon by designating 11 historic spa towns across the continent as a single transnational world heritage site. These grand destinations range from Bath in England to Spa in Belgium, as well as the renowned west Bohemia spa triangle.

Among the trio in west Bohemia, Mariánské Lázně stands out as particularly picturesque. Visitors here can experience three distinct natural healing traditions: mineral springs, carbon dioxide springs called Maria’s Gas, and therapeutic peloids such as mud and clay. Tourists frequently stroll along the colonnades while drinking the mineral water from special porcelain cups, often pairing the experience with crispy sweet spa wafers. Many historic locations throughout the region, including the canary yellow Nové Lázně hotel, feature preserved architecture that lets travelers step directly back into the 19th century. King Edward VII visited this famous hotel nine times, and a special treatment cabin was even built specifically for him.

Germany hosts hundreds of designated spa towns, with Bavaria's Bad Kissingen serving as a prime example of striking early 20th-century architecture designed by star architect Max Littmann. The town features a grand fountain hall with a stained-glass roof, where fountain women dispense various mineral waters from bronze pipes, alongside the Regentenbau, an art nouveau building housing one of the best concert halls in Europe. Music remains deeply integrated into the local culture, complementing traditional therapies like inhaling salt-infused air near graduation towers or soaking in brine spring waters pumped directly from the spring.

Further south, deep within the Black Forest, Bad Wildbad combines natural immersion with thermal treatments. Visitors can ride a funicular railway to the summit of Sommerberg, cross the extensive Wildline suspension bridge, or ascend the Treetop Walk for panoramic views above the dense pine trees. Afterward, guests can unwind in historic thermal baths surrounded by marble pillars and Moorish tiles, or visit modern facilities tailored for joint and movement therapy.

In Normandy, Bagnoles de l’Orne offers belle époque villas nestled around a forest lake. According to local legend, the resort's warm sulphurous waters were originally discovered by a medieval nobleman whose warhorse returned from the woods revitalized. Today, visitors can enjoy outdoor activities ranging from cycling and hiking to meditative autumn mushroom foraging before relaxing with localized body wraps and hydromassages.

Meanwhile, the Austrian alpine town of Bad Gastein was built around a roaring waterfall and radon-rich thermal springs that once attracted famous thinkers like Sigmund Freud. Although the original fashion for taking the waters temporarily waned, the town has experienced a vibrant revival with modernized hotels and brutalist public bath complexes. Similarly, Piešťany in Slovakia uses sulphurous mud applied at high temperatures for therapeutic packs, while Rogaška in Slovenia draws visitors eager to taste magnesium-rich mineral water straight from the source.

facts.fact: In 2021, Unesco designated 11 historic spa towns across Europe as a transnational world heritage site.
Mariánské Lázně in Czechia offers three natural healing traditions: mineral springs, carbon dioxide springs known as Maria’s Gas, and therapeutic peloids including mud and clay.
Bad Kissingen in Bavaria features architecture rebuilt by star German architect Max Littmann, including a grand fountain hall and the Regentenbau concert hall.
Bad Wildbad in the Black Forest offers the Treetop Walk, the Wildline suspension bridge, and historic thermal baths like the Palais Thermal.
Bagnoles de l’Orne in Normandy features belle époque villas on a lake, tied to a legend of a medieval lord's warhorse finding warm sulphurous waters.
Bad Gastein in the Austrian Alps features radon-rich thermal springs and historic hotels that once hosted figures like Sigmund Freud.
Piešťany in Slovakia is known for its thermal waters and sulphurous mud used in treatments at the Thermia Palace and Irma Balneotherapy House.
Rogaška in eastern Slovenia is famed for Donat Mg, a mineral water exceptionally rich in magnesium.
